paragraphs: The paper studies multiplication performed by recalling a memorized answer rather than following a calculation procedure. This kind of arithmetic can be difficult even though the underlying collection of basic facts is relatively small. The authors focus on the characteristic mistakes people make when retrieving multiplication facts, including both which wrong answers occur and how frequently errors happen.

They propose a model of this associative multiplication process and compare its behavior with human data. The comparison examines two aspects of performance: the kinds of errors produced and their frequency. The model is also compared with an earlier model by Anderson and colleagues, giving the investigation another computational account against which to assess its behavior.

The central contribution is an attempt to explain the structure of arithmetic errors through a model of memory-based multiplication. Matching correct answers alone would leave those patterns unexplained. The abstract establishes the proposed model and the comparisons undertaken, but does not report which model better matches human performance.
neurips-1998-a-model-for-associative-mul.tldr: The paper proposes a model of memorized multiplication and compares its error types and frequencies with human behavior and an earlier model.

paragraphs: A principal curve describes the central shape of a cloud of points using a curve rather than a single straight direction. The paper builds on a definition in which a continuous curve has a specified length and is chosen to minimize the average squared distance from randomly sampled points to the curve. This gives a precise objective for what passing through the data should mean.

The authors had previously used that definition to analyze how principal curves can be learned from training data. Here they turn the definition into a practical construction using a polygonal line. The contribution connects a mathematically specified fitting problem with an algorithm for constructing a curve from observations.

Simulations show favorable comparisons with earlier methods in both performance and computational complexity. These results support the practical usefulness of the construction alongside its theoretical motivation. The evidence is a simulation-based comparison: it indicates that the proposed formulation can lead to an effective algorithm, without establishing that it outperforms every alternative on every distribution.
neurips-1998-a-polygonal-line-algorithm-.tldr: A polygonal-line algorithm turns a length-constrained definition of principal curves into a practical method with favorable simulation results.

paragraphs: The paper asks how a system could discover objects, parts, and smaller subparts from visual experience without already knowing object categories. Its proposed principle compares regularities at different scales: relationships inside a part are more consistent than relationships between different parts of an object. That difference provides a basis for deciding which visual elements belong together.

Applying the principle repeatedly creates a hierarchy of part-whole relationships. A grouping found at one level can participate in a larger grouping at another level. The required evidence comes from statistics across sample scenes, rather than supplied object models or other higher-level knowledge. This makes the approach an account of how hierarchical organization could emerge through unsupervised learning.

The author illustrates the principle with a model that decomposes simple scenes. The model can also account for results from a human experiment concerning the development of part-whole relationships. These findings support the principle as an explanation of that demonstrated learning behavior, while the visual demonstrations themselves concern simple scenes.
neurips-1998-a-principle-for-unsupervise.tldr: The paper proposes learning visual hierarchies by grouping elements whose internal relationships are more regular than their relationships with other parts.

paragraphs: The paper develops a theory of mean field approximation using information geometry. Its aim is to provide a consistent account of several approaches used in statistical physics. The central move is to describe these approaches within a framework that connects their mathematical structure with information-theoretic meaning.

The theory encompasses the naive mean field approximation, the TAP approach, and the linear response theorem. Bringing all three into one account matters because the contribution is about their relationship, as well as their individual interpretation. The framework treats them as parts of a coherent theory and gives each a clear information-theoretic reading.

The stated result is therefore a conceptual and mathematical unification. It offers a way to understand how these established tools fit together through information geometry, with the emphasis on explaining their foundations. The abstract presents this unified interpretation as the contribution; it does not frame the work as an empirical comparison or report a new application's performance.
neurips-1998-a-theory-of-mean-field-appr.tldr: An information-geometric theory unifies naive mean field approximation, the TAP approach, and linear response with information-theoretic interpretations.

paragraphs: This paper applies a hierarchical pyramid neural network to two mammographic detection problems. The architecture combines neural networks with image processing at multiple scales. Its guiding idea is that evidence useful for detecting an object may occur at a different scale from the object itself, so information must be integrated across resolutions.

For small microcalcifications, the authors use a coarse-to-fine architecture designed to learn broader contextual information. Receiver operating characteristic analysis suggests that this improves the detection performance of an established computer-aided diagnosis system by roughly 50%. This is a reported improvement in detection performance, rather than a claim that accuracy rises by 50 percentage points.

For larger, extended masses, the authors instead construct a fine-to-coarse architecture to learn relevant small-scale detail. Initial results are encouraging, with an improvement of about 36%. Together, the applications support choosing the direction of information integration according to the detection problem: broad context can help locate small objects, while fine structure can help identify larger ones.
neurips-1998-applications-of-multi-resol.tldr: Multiscale neural networks show improved mammographic detection by using broad context for microcalcifications and fine detail for masses.

paragraphs: The paper introduces an iterative method for estimating the parameters of Gaussian mixture models. Its starting point is a framework developed by Kivinen and Warmuth for supervised online learning. The authors adapt that framework to mixture estimation, producing a procedure that can operate either on a batch of observations or in an online setting.

The distinctive design choice concerns the matrices describing each mixture component's spread and relationships among variables. Gradient descent and expectation maximization, or EM, estimate covariance matrices. The proposed method instead estimates their inverses. This changes which mathematical quantities the iterative procedure updates while retaining the goal of fitting a Gaussian mixture.

Experiments indicate that the method is typically faster than EM and usually needs about half as many iterations. These are qualified empirical findings, so they support a practical advantage in the reported comparisons rather than a universal speed guarantee. The combination of fewer iterations and support for both batch and online estimation is the paper's stated practical appeal.
neurips-1998-batch-and-on-line-parameter.tldr: An iterative Gaussian-mixture estimator updates inverse covariance matrices and typically converges faster than EM in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: The paper presents an analog integrated-circuit implementation for estimating motion across a two-dimensional visual field. It extends an earlier circuit for global motion sensing by also providing smooth optical flow. This means the implementation addresses a spatial pattern of apparent motion as well as the overall movement of the visual field.

Optical flow is an ill-posed problem: the available visual information does not by itself uniquely determine motion. The abstract identifies this ambiguity with the aperture problem. The approach addresses it through regularization, adding constraints expressed as a global energy function whose minimum corresponds to the desired motion estimate.

The key contribution is mapping the smoothness constraints of the Horn and Schunck algorithm onto physical constraints in an equivalent electronic network. This connects an algorithmic formulation of motion estimation with a feedback-connected analog implementation. The work shows how additional constraints used to resolve visual ambiguity can be embodied in circuit behavior, yielding both smooth optical flow and global motion estimates.
neurips-1998-computation-of-smooth-optic.tldr: The paper maps smooth optical-flow constraints onto an analog circuit that estimates both local flow and global motion.

paragraphs: The paper examines divisive normalization, a proposed visual-cortex mechanism that regulates neural responses through divisive inhibition. Its focus is what this operation does when neural activity contains noise. The authors ask whether normalization can help extract information from a population of neurons, beyond its role in shaping visual responses.

Simulations show that divisive normalization closely approximates maximum likelihood estimation. In the population-coding setting considered, this corresponds to an ideal observer's readout of noisy activity. The authors also provide an analytical result connecting this estimation ability to a large class of nonlinear recurrent networks with line attractors.

The findings suggest that normalization itself can perform much of the information extraction otherwise assigned to a separate ideal-observer stage. This gives the mechanism a possible role in filtering noise as information moves through cortical processing. The broader proposal is that each cortical layer may act as an ideal observer of the preceding layer; that biological interpretation remains a suggestion, distinct from the simulation and analytical results.
neurips-1998-divisive-normalization-line.tldr: Simulations and analysis connect divisive normalization with near-ideal estimation of noisy neural activity, suggesting a cortical noise-filtering role.

paragraphs: The paper studies how supervised learning evolves in layered neural networks when the training set remains restricted relative to the network's input size. Specifically, the number of training examples is proportional to the number of inputs. This makes the ratio between data size and input size a central feature of the analysis.

In this regime, the local fields involved in the learning dynamics no longer have Gaussian distributions. The authors use dynamical replica theory to predict the evolution of macroscopic observables, including relevant error measures. The emphasis is on describing aggregate learning behavior over time while accounting for the distributional structure of the restricted-data setting.

The resulting theory also incorporates the earlier formalism when the ratio of training examples to inputs grows without bound. This connects the restricted-training-set analysis with the large-data limit. The contribution is a theoretical description that handles the stated proportional-size regime while recovering the previous account in the limiting case where training data becomes comparatively abundant.
neurips-1998-dynamics-of-supervised-lear.tldr: Dynamical replica theory describes supervised-learning dynamics when training-set size is proportional to input size and local fields are non-Gaussian.

paragraphs: Physics-based animation can produce realistic motion, but numerically simulating the underlying dynamics can be computationally expensive. This paper explores replacing that numerical simulation with a neural-network emulator called a NeuroAnimator. The objective is to retain physically realistic animation while reducing the computation required to generate motion.

A NeuroAnimator is trained automatically offline by observing a physics-based model in action. The network learns to emulate the model's dynamics from those observations. This places the learning stage before the animation stage in which the emulator is used, allowing the trained network to serve as a faster substitute for conventional numerical simulation.

The authors demonstrate the approach on a variety of physics-based models, including nontrivial dynamic systems. Depending on the model, the emulator can produce physically realistic animation one or two orders of magnitude faster than conventional simulation. The result establishes the possibility of substantial speed improvements through learned emulation, with the size of the benefit explicitly depending on the model being animated.
neurips-1998-fast-neural-network-emulati.tldr: NeuroAnimators learn physical dynamics offline and can generate realistic animation 10–100 times faster than numerical simulation, depending on the model.

paragraphs: The paper asks how much experience Q-learning and a model-based reinforcement-learning approach need to produce a near-optimal policy. The model-based method estimates next-state distributions and then performs offline value iteration. The authors compare the two approaches through finite-sample guarantees, measuring experience by the number of observed state transitions.

In an idealized model where transitions are well mixed across an N-state Markov decision process, both approaches have roughly the same sample complexity. The stated sufficient bound grows approximately linearly with N and inversely with the square of the desired error tolerance, with additional logarithmic factors. Achieving a good policy requires substantially less data than accurately reconstructing the next-state distribution, and the model-based memory requirement is closer to linear than quadratic in N.

The authors also consider transitions generated by a fixed, arbitrary exploration policy. This removes the idealized well-mixed assumption, but makes the bounds depend on that policy's stationary distribution and mixing time. The results therefore distinguish learning from broadly distributed experience from learning under a particular exploration process.
neurips-1998-finite-sample-convergence-r.tldr: Finite-sample bounds give Q-learning and model-based learning similar sample complexity under well-mixed sampling, with exploration-dependent bounds beyond that setting.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a neural-network training strategy based on sequential sampling and importance resampling. It frames training as a global optimization problem and uses a sequential procedure to learn a probability distribution over the network's weights. The distribution over weights is therefore a central object of the method.

This formulation brings together network training and probabilistic estimation in a process that proceeds sequentially. Sampling and importance resampling provide the stated algorithmic basis for that process. The approach matters because it describes training in terms of learning about possible weight settings through a distribution, giving the optimization strategy an explicitly probabilistic form.

The authors identify online, nonlinear, non-Gaussian, and nonstationary signal processing as suitable applications. Those settings motivate a method that can operate sequentially while accommodating the kinds of signal behavior named in the abstract. The stated contribution is the training strategy and its suitability for those applications; the description of global optimization does not itself assert guaranteed recovery of a global optimum.
neurips-1998-global-optimisation-of-neur.tldr: The paper proposes sequential sampling and importance resampling to train neural networks by learning a distribution over their weights.

paragraphs: The paper derives Value and Policy Search, or VAPS, as a learning rule that generates a broad family of reinforcement-learning algorithms. Its aim is to place value-based learning and direct policy search within one theory. These approaches can then be used individually or combined through the same general construction.

The generated algorithms include modifications of Q-learning, SARSA, and advantage learning. Their original forms can fail to converge on simple Markov decision processes when using parameterized value-function approximators. The paper reports convergence guarantees for the algorithms produced by its framework. It also includes pure policy-search methods that learn optimal policies without first learning a value function.

The framework extends to partially observable Markov decision processes, where the stated convergence does not require a proper belief state. Simulations accompany the theoretical development. The main significance is a common route to constructing and combining learning algorithms with convergence guarantees; convergence and optimal-policy learning are distinct claims in the abstract and should not be collapsed into one universal guarantee.
neurips-1998-gradient-descent-for-genera.tldr: VAPS unifies value-based learning and policy search through a general learning rule that produces algorithms with convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: A robot may already have controllers for useful subtasks yet still need to decide how to combine them into a successful overall behavior. This paper formulates that problem using Markov and semi-Markov decision processes. A temporally extended action, called an option, consists of a controller together with a condition that determines when it stops.

The authors present a theorem about the performance improvement available through flexible switching among given controllers. They show how planning with these high-level actions can provide information for improving the plan further by modifying the controllers. This additional improvement can be obtained with negligible extra cost and without repeating the planning process.

Examples illustrate the theorem and the computational benefit of working at the controller level. In one example, the problem shrinks from 24 billion state-action pairs to fewer than one million state-controller pairs. The contribution combines a manageable planning representation with a way to improve how existing behaviors are used, so their original boundaries need not determine the final policy.
neurips-1998-improved-switching-among-te.tldr: Planning with existing controllers can support improved switching and controller modification without replanning, while greatly reducing one example's planning representation.

paragraphs: Local search for combinatorial optimization uses an evaluation of candidate solutions to guide its progress. This paper uses reinforcement learning to learn an evaluation function that predicts the outcome of further search. Such a function can guide the algorithm toward low-cost solutions better than the original cost function, which evaluates the solution currently under consideration.

The authors learn this value function in an offline phase. A central goal is reuse: the learned function is useful across multiple problem instances and sizes. The method combines aspects of earlier reinforcement-learning approaches to enhancing local search, making the learned guidance applicable beyond a single search problem.

The technique is illustrated by developing several value functions for the Dial-A-Ride Problem. The resulting learning-enhanced search shows an improvement of more than 30% over a standard local-search algorithm. This supports the usefulness of learning predictions about search outcomes and transferring that guidance across instances, while the reported percentage is a performance improvement whose specific measurement is not identified in the abstract.
neurips-1998-learning-instance-independe.tldr: Offline reinforcement learning produces reusable value functions that improve local search, with a reported improvement above 30% on Dial-A-Ride problems.

paragraphs: The paper studies how a reinforcement-learning agent can construct macro-actions from its primitive actions while it learns. The agent starts without a supplied collection of these larger behaviors. The method builds them through experience, using reward to strengthen useful patterns in the order that actions are performed.

Its central rule reinforces the tendency to take action b after action a when that pattern has been rewarded. This gives a simple mechanism for turning successful action combinations into larger units of behavior. The authors test the method on bicycle, car-on-the-hill, race-track, and grid-world tasks to examine whether these learned combinations reduce learning time.

The effects differ across tasks. Macro-actions approximately halve learning time for the bicycle and race-track tasks, and reduce it by a factor of five in one grid-world task. The method does not work for the car-on-the-hill task. The findings therefore support substantial benefits in some settings while showing that rewarded action chaining is not effective across all the tested problems.
neurips-1998-learning-macro-actions-in-r.tldr: Learning macro-actions from rewarded action sequences speeds learning substantially on several tasks but fails on the tested car-on-the-hill task.

paragraphs: The paper develops a common way to prove relative loss bounds for online linear threshold classifiers, including Perceptron and Winnow. In this setting, the discrete loss is the total number of prediction mistakes. The challenge addressed is how to connect the algorithms' updates with mathematical guarantees expressed in that mistake count.

The authors introduce a continuous quantity called linear hinge loss. It can be used to derive algorithm updates and serves as the first target of their analysis. They establish relative bounds for this continuous loss before translating those results into bounds for discrete prediction errors. This provides a shared analytical route for the classification algorithms considered.

The translation uses a newly introduced notion of the average margin of a collection of examples. Average margin links the continuous-loss analysis to the mistake-count guarantee. The contribution is thus both a loss-based method of analysis and a way to express its consequences in the original classification measure, giving different online algorithms a common theoretical treatment.
neurips-1998-linear-hinge-loss-and-avera.tldr: Linear hinge loss and average margin provide a unified route from continuous-loss bounds to mistake bounds for online linear classifiers.

paragraphs: The paper introduces two techniques for estimating a probability density by reformulating the problem as supervised learning. This allows neural networks to perform the learning task. The key change is how the estimation problem is posed, giving a supervised-learning procedure a role in recovering the distribution represented by the observations.

One technique uses a stochastic method to learn the cumulative distribution, and the other is an analogous deterministic technique. The cumulative distribution describes accumulated probability, providing the quantity around which the proposed learning approach is constructed. Presenting both versions gives two related ways to pursue the same density-estimation objective.

The authors demonstrate convergence theoretically and experimentally, and compare their methods with the Parzen estimate. Their theoretical results establish better convergence properties than that reference method. This supports the mathematical promise of the reformulation alongside experimental evidence of convergence. The stated advantage concerns convergence properties; it does not establish that every finite dataset or implementation will yield better estimates or lower computational cost.
neurips-1998-neural-networks-for-density.tldr: Two neural-network density-estimation techniques recast the task as supervised learning and have better theoretical convergence properties than the Parzen estimate.

paragraphs: The paper addresses how a neural network can preserve memory performance while losing many synapses. Mammalian development motivates the question, since substantial synaptic pruning occurs during childhood. Earlier work by the authors indicated that preserving performance requires appropriate changes to the remaining connections and preferential removal of weaker synapses.

Here they examine neuronal regulation, a mechanism observed to maintain the average input field of a neuron. They show that it produces synaptic changes that depend on connection strength. Within the correct range of the degradation dimension and the upper bound on synaptic strength, the mechanism removes weaker connections and modifies those that remain.

Under those stated conditions, neuronal regulation implements nearly optimal synaptic modification and maintains memory performance through extensive pruning. This provides a possible mechanism linking regulation of neuronal input to useful restructuring of network connections. The broader developmental conclusion is qualified: alongside Hebbian changes, neuronal regulation may play an important role in how brain networks organize themselves as they mature.
neurips-1998-neuronal-regulation-impleme.tldr: Under suitable parameter conditions, neuronal regulation preferentially prunes weak synapses while modifying surviving connections to preserve network memory.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a nonlinear modification of proportional-integral control inspired by a signaling pathway involved in mammalian blood-pressure regulation. The method is called proportional with intermittent integral, or PII. It targets systems that require exact matching of a desired operating value while attenuating disturbances, with infrequent step changes in either load disturbances or the desired value.

The proportional controller is designed independently to attenuate disturbances. Integral control is then activated intermittently to achieve exact set-point matching. Mechanisms observed in the Angiotensin II/AT1 pathway motivate how the algorithm switches that integral action. This separates the two control roles while coordinating when the integral component operates.

The authors demonstrate improved performance over conventional PI control on a model of cyclopentenol production. At the desired operating point, a change in the sign of plant gain makes traditional PI control unstable. The proposed approach achieves stable, exact matching for achievable set-points in this example, supporting intermittent integral control for the particular control difficulty studied.
neurips-1998-non-linear-pi-control-inspi.tldr: A biologically inspired controller activates integral control intermittently, achieving stable set-point matching in a production model where traditional PI becomes unstable.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a probabilistic framework for visualizing high-dimensional data, with particular attention to binary and categorical observations. These data types are a central motivation because few established visualization methods were available for them in the setting described. The framework uses latent variables to support the visualization within a probabilistic model.

The authors derive a fast procedure for determining the model parameters by using a variational approximation to the likelihood. Parameter fitting is therefore tied to an approximation of the model's probabilistic objective. This is the main computational ingredient identified in the abstract and explains how the proposed framework is made practical to fit.

Applications to both real and synthetic binary datasets illustrate the method. These examples demonstrate its use on binary observations, while the framework itself is described as applicable to categorical data as well. The contribution combines a visualization model suited to these discrete data types with a fast parameter-estimation procedure, bringing the representation and its fitting method into one probabilistic approach.
neurips-1998-probabilistic-visualisation.tldr: A probabilistic latent-variable framework visualizes binary and categorical data using a fast fitting algorithm derived from a variational likelihood approximation.

paragraphs: The paper applies Gaussian mixture modeling to three-dimensional range data used by a mobile robot. Expectation maximization fits the model, producing a probabilistic summary of the sensor observations. The approach is intended to handle uncertainty in sensing and allow prior knowledge to influence low-level perception in the robot-docking setting.

The authors address problems with the basic method in two ways. They change the mixture's parameterization to reflect the kinds of objects expected in a scene, and incorporate priors on model parameters into optimization. These choices steer the fitted model toward objects of interest given the sensor characteristics and the expected object structure.

A higher-level classifier then interprets the model's output and rejects spurious solutions. The resulting approach combines probabilistic data summarization, object-informed fitting, and subsequent classification. Its significance is that obtaining a useful scene interpretation involves more than fitting a generic mixture: knowledge about the expected objects guides optimization, and a separate interpretation stage filters out misleading results.
neurips-1998-robot-docking-using-mixture.tldr: Gaussian mixtures summarize robot range data, with object-specific parameterization, priors, and a higher-level classifier guiding useful interpretations.

paragraphs: The paper studies the long-run behavior of autoregressive neural-network processes. Its central question is stationarity: whether the process approaches behavior whose statistical properties remain stable over time. The authors analyze this question using methods from Markov-chain theory and nonlinear time-series analysis, linking neural-network models with established tools for studying evolving stochastic processes.

For standard autoregressive neural networks without shortcut connections, the authors show asymptotic stationarity. The qualification matters: the result concerns long-run behavior, rather than asserting that the process has stationary statistics from its initial state. The architecture without shortcuts is one of the two cases distinguished in the analysis.

When linear shortcut connections are included, the shortcut weights alone determine whether the overall system is stationary. Consequently, standard stationarity conditions for linear autoregressive processes can be applied. This gives a particularly direct way to assess the long-run behavior of the combined system: the relevant condition is governed by the linear shortcuts even though the model also contains a neural-network component.
neurips-1998-stationarity-and-stability-.tldr: Standard autoregressive neural networks are asymptotically stationary, while stationarity with linear shortcuts is determined solely by the shortcut weights.

paragraphs: Face recognition involves choosing among many known individuals, whereas a support vector machine directly separates two classes. The paper resolves this mismatch by representing differences between pairs of facial images. In this difference space, the two classes indicate whether the images belong to the same person or to different people.

The authors reinterpret the SVM's decision surface to obtain a learned measure of facial similarity. Training on image differences therefore supplies a comparison between faces that can support recognition involving multiple identities. The central contribution is this reformulation and interpretation of the classifier's output.

On a difficult image set from the FERET database, the method is compared with a principal-component-analysis approach in both identification and verification settings. Identification performance is 77–78% for the SVM method and 54% for PCA. For verification, equal error rates are 7% and 13%, respectively. These results favor the SVM approach on the evaluated image set and show benefits for both deciding identity and checking a proposed identity.
neurips-1998-support-vector-machines-app.tldr: An SVM trained on differences between face images learns a similarity measure and outperforms PCA on the reported identification and verification tests.

paragraphs: The paper investigates mutual information between model parameters and observations. This quantity concerns how much the data reveal about the parameters. The motivation comes from work in parameter estimation and neural coding that relates optimal performance to this information, making it a useful object for theoretical analysis.

The authors focus on a particular model structure: the conditional probability density of an observation depends on the parameter vector only through its scalar product with that observation. This restriction specifies exactly how the parameters enter the observation model. The resulting analysis therefore concerns this structured dependence rather than arbitrary relationships between parameters and data.

Within that setting, the authors derive bounds and asymptotic behavior for mutual information. They also compare their results with those obtained using the replica technique on the same model. The contribution is a mathematical characterization of parameter-observation information and a comparison between analytical approaches, providing results tied to the stated scalar-product assumption.
neurips-1998-unsupervised-and-supervised.tldr: The paper bounds parameter-observation mutual information for a scalar-product-dependent model and compares its asymptotic results with replica calculations.
